name: Mineral water
anchor: strictest applicable sovereign drinking-water or packaged-water maximum, per litre of finished product as consumed, with natural mineral water kept as the separate product form the instruments themselves treat it as (Hong Kong Cap 132V writes dedicated natural-mineral-water lines; EU Directive 2020/2184 excludes the form from its scope)
cross_reference: A naturally carbonated natural mineral water is governed by THIS row, not by the sparkling/carbonated-water row: its legal product form, not its carbonation, determines the applicable instrument. Mineralised or mineral-fortified purified water is not natural mineral water and routes to the bottled-drinking-water row.
native_basis_label: as consumed, per litre of natural mineral water in its packaged state (µg/L; numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
scope_note: In scope: natural mineral water as defined by the recognising authority — water from a protected underground source, bottled at source, of consistent characterising mineral composition, sold without treatment beyond those the instrument permits. This is a legally distinct product form, not a marketing label, and it is the one row of this category where the packaged-water bridge is partly switched off: EU Directive 2020/2184 expressly excludes natural mineral waters recognised under Directive 2009/54/EC from its scope, so no Drinking Water Directive value is used here. The instruments that do reach this form are FDA 21 CFR 165.110 (US law defines mineral water as a type of bottled water at s.165.110(a)(2)(iii), so the standards of quality apply, save that mineral water is exempt from the aesthetically based secondary levels) and the dedicated natural-mineral-water lines of Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Chile Decreto 977/1996 and Fiji FSR 2009. Commission Directive 2003/40/EC also reaches this form and is the EU's operative natural-mineral-water metals instrument, but it is ABSENT from data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, so it anchors nothing on this row and no value is asserted for it. REGISTER GAP ON THIS ROW: 2003/40/EC is absent from the candidate set of every cell here, which is why no cell on this row cites an EU natural-mineral-water instrument; it is logged as a register gap for retrieval and ingest through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway, and every cell on this row is recompiled against it when it lands. It is the instrument a reviewer will look for first on this row, and its absence is disclosed rather than passed over. Two row-level differences from the other packaged-water rows are recorded with their true mechanism rather than a convenient one. Total chromium is 50 µg/L here against 25 µg/L on the other rows, and that is a SCOPE consequence, not an instrument-written split: Hong Kong Cap 132V writes 50 µg/L for both packaged-water forms, and the difference exists only because Directive 2020/2184 excludes natural mineral water, so the Directive's 25 µg/L is not an applicable maximum here. Nickel is the genuine instrument-written split, Hong Kong writing 20 µg/L for natural mineral waters against 70 µg/L for other packaged drinking waters, and that split is honoured in the anchor selection on this row, although it produces no published difference because the Directive independently puts the other rows at 20 µg/L. Where an instrument writes a split it is preserved rather than smoothed; where none exists none is manufactured. Out of scope: mineral-fortified or mineralised purified water, which is not natural mineral water and routes to the bottled-drinking-water row or, if flavoured, to Category 5; nothing on the basis of carbonation alone — a naturally carbonated natural mineral water stays on this row.
basis_guard: ^(?!.*(dry weight|dry matter|dehydrated|migration|leach|material content|surface|\bfeed\b|fat basis))(?=.*(water|as[ _]?consumed|mg/l|placed on market|food as listed)).*$
basis_guard_note: Every named anchor must be a dietary per-litre / as-consumed water or food-schedule basis. The guard rejects dry-weight, dehydrated, migration/leachate, article material-content and feed bases outright, so a dry-commodity maximum level or a food-contact migration limit can never anchor a per-litre water cell. It admits mg/kg-expressed food-schedule rows (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011) because potable water density is within 0.3 per cent of 1 kg/L, so µg/kg and µg/L are the same number to well inside analytical uncertainty; that is a stated identity, not a silent conversion.
method: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit default; strictest applicable sovereign maximum for the exact packaged-water form in its native per-litre as-consumed basis, disclosed read-across where the exact cell is unregulated, control where no defensible sovereign number exists; never occurrence-derived)

Pb.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Pb.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for natural mineral water (FDA 21 CFR 165.110, which covers mineral water as a defined bottled-water type)
Pb.substantiation: Lead at 5 µg/L is compelled by FDA 21 CFR 165.110: in US law mineral water is a defined type of bottled water (s.165.110(a)(2)(iii)) and the standards of quality apply to it, so the 0.005 mg/L allowable level is a direct maximum for this product form, not a read-across. It is matched by the Health Canada maximum acceptable concentration and the NHMRC health-based guideline value under the packaged-water bridge. Every mineral-water-specific line in the pool is looser at 10 µg/L (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011) or 50 µg/L (Fiji FSR 2009); all are named and none is selected. The EU Drinking Water Directive value is not used on this row because the Directive excludes natural mineral water from its scope. REGISTER GAP ON THIS CELL: Commission Directive 2003/40/EC, the EU instrument that sets metals limits for natural mineral waters (Directive 2009/54/EC defines the product but sets no metals values), is absent from data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv and is therefore absent from this cell's candidate set; it is logged as a register gap and no value is asserted for it. The row's scope note records the gap in full.

Cd.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Cd.label: disclosed read-across from the NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines health-based guideline value; the ADWG governs drinking-water supplies rather than packaged product, and Australia's packaged-water cadmium cell is absent from the register
Cd.substantiation: Cadmium at 2 µg/L is the NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines health-based guideline value (0.002 mg/L, nhmrc2025_cd_drinking_water_2), the strictest cadmium value any government sets for water. It is published as a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS and not as a direct maximum for this product form, and the reason is stated rather than left to inference. The register records that instrument's product scope as 'drinking water' and its note describes it as a health-based guideline value; the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines are a non-statutory guideline for drinking-water supplies, and Australia regulates packaged water not under the ADWG but under the FSANZ Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code. No FSANZ packaged-water metals row exists in the register: of the AU, NZ and AU-NZ rows, the only water-scoped entries are the eight NHMRC drinking-water guideline values, and Schedule 19 is represented only by commodity rows (formula, cereals, fish, salt and the like). The Australian packaged-water cadmium cell is therefore absent from the register and is logged as a register gap, in the same way Commission Directive 2003/40/EC is logged on the mineral-water row. The category's two textual packaged-water bridges do not carry this instrument either: FDA 21 CFR 165.110(b)(4)(iii) incorporates the EPA maximum contaminant levels (cadmium 5 µg/L) and EU Directive 2020/2184's scope reaches water put into bottles or containers (cadmium 5 µg/L), and neither reaches an Australian guideline. Absence of a packaged-product carve-out is not affirmative scope, so the earlier regulatory-alignment tag overstated what this instrument does. WHAT THE INSTRUMENTS SET FOR THE EXACT CELL IS STATED OPENLY, because the read-across runs in the protective direction and nothing is served by concealing it: the strictest maximum level any government sets for cadmium in this exact packaged-water form is 3 µg/L, then 5 µg/L (EU Drinking Water Directive eu20202184_cd_drinking_water_5, FDA 21 CFR 165.110 fda21cfr165110_cd_bottled_water_5, EPA MCL epa2018_cd_drinking_water_5, California us_ca_swrcb_2024_cd_cadmium_mcl_5ugl), then 7 µg/L (Health Canada healthcanada2025_cd_drinking_water_7). HMTc publishes the stricter 2 µg/L: the substance and the basis are identical, HMTc does not relax a published limit toward a looser instrument, and the value is unchanged from the earlier compilation. Only the provenance tag is corrected, from regulatory-alignment to read-across, so that the record never claims a sovereign packaged-water maximum that no sovereign has written. The mineral-water-specific lines cluster at 3 µg/L (Hong Kong Cap 132V hk_cap132v_cd_natural-mineral-waters_3, India FSSAI 2016 in_fssai2016_cd_014_natural_mineral_water_3, GSO 193/2021 gso193_2021_cd_natural_mineral_waters_3, Colombia Res 4506/2013 co_res4506_2013_cd_mineral_water_3, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011 vn_qcvn8_2_2011_cd_natural-mineral-water_3, Israel FCS 2016 il_fcs2016_cd_17_bottled_drinking_water_and_mineral_water_3), with Fiji FSR 2009 at 5 µg/L and Chile Decreto 977/1996 at 10 µg/L. Cadmium is a contaminant, not a characterising mineral constituent, so nothing in the natural-mineral-water product definition makes the stricter drinking-water value inapplicable. REGISTER GAP ON THIS CELL: Commission Directive 2003/40/EC, the EU instrument that sets metals limits for natural mineral waters, is absent from data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv and is therefore absent from this cell's candidate set; it is logged as a register gap and no value is asserted for it.

tAs.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
tAs.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for natural mineral water (Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2 item 2, natural-mineral-waters line)
tAs.substantiation: Total arsenic at 10 µg/L is unanimous across every mineral-water-specific line in the pool (Hong Kong Cap 132V, India FSSAI 2016, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, Israel FCS 2016) and across the packaged-water and drinking-water instruments that reach this form (FDA 21 CFR 165.110, NHMRC, Health Canada, WHO). Only Fiji is looser at 50 µg/L. There is no stricter sovereign total-arsenic value for mineral water anywhere in the register. REGISTER GAP ON THIS CELL: Commission Directive 2003/40/EC, the EU instrument that sets metals limits for natural mineral waters (Directive 2009/54/EC defines the product but sets no metals values), is absent from data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv and is therefore absent from this cell's candidate set; it is logged as a register gap and no value is asserted for it. The row's scope note records the gap in full.

iAs.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
iAs.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for the exact product form (Israel FCS 2016 row 16.1, whose scope names mineral water expressly)
iAs.substantiation: Inorganic arsenic at 6 µg/L is the Israel FCS 2016 maximum level for the exact product form ('Bottled drinking water and mineral water', source row 16.1, 0.006 mg/kg), the strictest sovereign inorganic-arsenic maximum for packaged water in the register. The alternatives are the US EPA drinking-water MCL recorded as inorganic arsenic at 10 µg/L and the Chilean Decreto 977/1996 Article 160 value of 10 µg/L for mineral and packaged drinking waters; both are named and neither is selected because 6 µg/L is applicable and stricter. The species cell is retained separately from total arsenic even though arsenic in potable water is effectively all inorganic, because the HMTc panel never allows a species to satisfy a total: a lot must clear both 10 µg/L total arsenic and 6 µg/L inorganic arsenic. Both named alternatives reach mineral water expressly: the Chilean value covers 'aguas minerales y aguas envasadas para bebida' and the EPA MCL reaches bottled mineral water through the FDA incorporation.

tHg.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
tHg.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for natural mineral water (Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2 item 12, natural-mineral-waters line)
tHg.substantiation: Total mercury at 1 µg/L is set for the exact product form by Hong Kong Cap 132V, India FSSAI 2016, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011 and Israel FCS 2016, and is matched by the NHMRC and Health Canada drinking-water values. The looser candidates are FDA 21 CFR 165.110 and Fiji FSR 2009 at 2 µg/L; both are named and neither is selected. Total mercury is published as a total and is never satisfied by a methylmercury or inorganic-mercury result. REGISTER GAP ON THIS CELL: Commission Directive 2003/40/EC, the EU instrument that sets metals limits for natural mineral waters (Directive 2009/54/EC defines the product but sets no metals values), is absent from data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv and is therefore absent from this cell's candidate set; it is logged as a register gap and no value is asserted for it. The row's scope note records the gap in full.

MeHg.rationale: Mercury in sealed packaged drinking water is present essentially as inorganic Hg(II). Methylation is a microbial process requiring anaerobic sulfate- or iron-reducing activity in sediment or biota; it does not occur in a treated, filtered, disinfected and sealed packaged-water matrix, and there is no aquatic food chain in the product to bioaccumulate methylmercury. Methylmercury is in any event a component of total mercury, so it is bounded by identity at the published total-mercury ceiling of 1 µg/L. No separate methylmercury ceiling is published.
MeHg.reference_method: Methylmercury is not separately quantified as a routine cell. Total mercury is measured on every certification lot by cold-vapour atomic fluorescence or ICP-MS against the published total-mercury ceiling. Where a lot result reaches or exceeds half the total-mercury ceiling, speciation by GC-ICP-MS or HPLC-ICP-MS is run as a reflex and the source water is investigated; a detectable methyl fraction is an immediate non-conformance regardless of the total-mercury result.
MeHg.regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction in the register sets a methylmercury maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water: of the 27 methylmercury rows in data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, every one is a fish or aquatic-animal tissue limit and none is water-scoped. Every drinking-water and packaged-water instrument in the pool regulates mercury as total mercury with no methyl line, and Hong Kong Cap 132V regulates the packaged-drinking-water mercury cell as INORGANIC mercury (0.006 mg/kg, hk_cap132v_ihg_bottled-or-packaged-drinking-waters-other-than-natural_6), which is direct sovereign confirmation that the regulated mercury species in packaged water is the inorganic one. The only methylmercury maxima anywhere in the register are fish and aquatic-animal limits (for example fda_cpg540600_mehg_fish_1000), which govern a bioaccumulating tissue matrix and have no application to water.
MeHg.jurisdictions_checked: EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I; EU Commission Directive 2003/40/EC (natural mineral waters — ABSENT from the register and logged as a register gap; this determination does not rest on it, and it is re-tested when the instrument is ingested); US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 165.110; California SWRCB Title 22 s.64431; Health Canada Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality (2025 summary tables); NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines; WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality; Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2; Israel FCS 2016; India FSSAI 2016; Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011; GSO 193/2021; Colombia Res 4506/2013; Chile Decreto 977/1996; Fiji FSR 2009.

Ni.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Ni.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for natural mineral water (Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2 item 14, natural-mineral-waters line)
Ni.substantiation: Nickel at 20 µg/L is the Hong Kong Cap 132V maximum for the exact product form, matched by the NHMRC health-based guideline value. Hong Kong writes a product-form split here that runs the other way from the usual pattern: 20 µg/L for natural mineral waters against 70 µg/L for other packaged drinking waters, reflecting that a natural mineral water is bottled at source without the treatment stages that can add nickel. The looser candidates (WHO 70 µg/L; FDA 21 CFR 165.110 and California at 100 µg/L, both descending from the EPA nickel MCL remanded in 1995) are named and not selected. The EU Drinking Water Directive value of 20 µg/L is not used on this row because the Directive excludes natural mineral water, but it corroborates the number. REGISTER GAP ON THIS CELL: Commission Directive 2003/40/EC, the EU instrument that sets metals limits for natural mineral waters (Directive 2009/54/EC defines the product but sets no metals values), is absent from data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv and is therefore absent from this cell's candidate set; it is logged as a register gap and no value is asserted for it. The row's scope note records the gap in full.

Sn.rationale: No sovereign sets a tin maximum for drinking water, bottled water or natural mineral water. The drinking-water instrument family carries no tin parameter at all (EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I Parts B and C; US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations; US FDA 21 CFR 165.110 standards of quality; Health Canada; NHMRC; WHO), and none of the national food-schedule packaged-water lines (Hong Kong Cap 132V, Israel FCS 2016, India FSSAI 2016, Vietnam QCVN 8-2:2011, GSO 193/2021, Colombia Res 4506/2013, Chile Decreto 977/1996, Fiji FSR 2009) carries a tin entry for water. A read-across is not supportable: the nearest sovereign tin maxima are the canned-food and canned-beverage maximum levels, which exist to bound dissolution of tin from a tinplate container wall into an acidic canned matrix, and the canned-beverage value (100 mg/kg inorganic tin) sits roughly four orders of magnitude above anything a packaged water can plausibly contain, so importing it would publish a ceiling that functions as no limit at all. The dominant packaging for this category (PET, HDPE, glass, aluminium) contains no tin. Natural mineral water is bottled at source in glass or PET; tinplate presentation does not occur in this form. Tin therefore remains a mandatory control cell; no number is invented.
Sn.reference_method: Tin by ICP-MS on the finished packaged product in its native per-litre as-consumed basis, on every certification lot, reported against the method limit of quantification rather than a ceiling. Any quantifiable tin result triggers investigation of the container, closure and liner, the filling line and the source water, and lot release is withheld pending root-cause identification and a clean re-test. Where the product is presented in a tinplate or tin-coated container, the EU canned-beverage inorganic-tin maximum level recorded as the companion instrument applies as a regulatory hard stop in addition to this control.

companions.scope: canned beverages, including canned fruit and vegetable juices, except ca

Al.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Al.label: disclosed read-across from the packaged-drinking-water aluminium parameter; no government sets a direct aluminium maximum for natural mineral water
Al.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated, and that is verifiable from the instruments' own text rather than from silence: FDA 21 CFR 165.110 sets aluminium only as a secondary, aesthetically based allowable level and expressly EXEMPTS mineral water from aesthetically based allowable levels; EU Directive 2020/2184, whose Annex I Part C indicator parameter is 200 µg/L, excludes natural mineral water from its scope; and the EU instrument that does govern natural mineral water, Commission Directive 2003/40/EC, is ABSENT from data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, so it supplies no value to this cell and none is asserted for it; it is logged as a register gap and this read-across is revisited when it is ingested. The nearest applicable sovereign value is therefore the 200 µg/L packaged-drinking-water aluminium parameter, read across here and matched independently by the NHMRC aesthetic guideline of 200 µg/L. The alternatives that could have been read across are far looser (California 1000 µg/L; Health Canada 2900 µg/L), so this is the strictest supportable analog, not a convenient one. As on the other rows, 200 µg/L is an indicator / secondary / aesthetic parameter and is labelled as such rather than presented as a toxicological line.

Cr.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Cr.label: strictest applicable sovereign maximum for natural mineral water (Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2 item 7, natural-mineral-waters line)
Cr.substantiation: Total chromium at 50 µg/L for natural mineral water is the Hong Kong Cap 132V Part 2 item 7 maximum for the exact product form, matched by Health Canada, the WHO guideline value and the California MCL. The EU Drinking Water Directive value of 25 µg/L is NOT applied to this row: Directive 2020/2184 expressly excludes natural mineral waters recognised under Directive 2009/54/EC from its scope, so 25 µg/L is not an applicable maximum for this product form. That is a product-form split written by the government rule itself, and the method requires it to be preserved rather than smoothed away. The applicable EU instrument for natural mineral water is Commission Directive 2003/40/EC, which is absent from data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv and is logged as a register gap. NO VALUE IS ASSERTED FOR IT: every number in this standard traces to a named register row, and an instrument that is not in the register supplies no number, so nothing is claimed here about what its chromium value is or whether it corroborates the Hong Kong anchor. When it is retrieved and ingested through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway this cell is recompiled against it, and if its chromium value is stricter than 50 µg/L the published value moves down. Note also that the 50-versus-25 difference against the other rows of this category is a scope consequence and not an instrument-written split: Hong Kong Cap 132V itself writes 50 µg/L for both packaged-water forms, and the Directive's 25 µg/L is excluded here only because the Directive excludes this product form. Published as a firm limit for the reason given on the other rows of this category.

Cr-VI.basis: µg/L of finished packaged water, as consumed (numerically equal to µg/kg at unit density)
Cr-VI.label: disclosed read-across from the California SWRCB Title 22 s.64431 hexavalent-chromium maximum contaminant level for public water systems; no government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum for any packaged-water form
Cr-VI.substantiation: The exact cell is unregulated, and the record says so on its face rather than asserting a maximum no government has written for this product form. No jurisdiction in the register sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum for bottled water, packaged water or natural mineral water, and neither of the two textual packaged-water bridges this category relies on reaches the species: FDA 21 CFR 165.110(b)(4)(iii) incorporates the EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulation maximum contaminant levels and EPA sets no hexavalent-chromium MCL, and EU Directive 2020/2184 Annex I carries no hexavalent-chromium parameter. The nearest applicable sovereign value is therefore the California State Water Resources Control Board Title 22 section 64431 Table 64431-A maximum contaminant level of 10 µg/L (0.01 mg/L, us_ca_swrcb_2024_cr-vi_chromium-hexavalent_mcl_10ugl), re-adopted in 2024 after health-risk and feasibility analysis, and it is carried across as a DISCLOSED READ-ACROSS. Two hops are disclosed rather than argued around. First, SCOPE: the register records that instrument's product scope as 'public water systems in California', which is utility-delivered tap water and not a packaged good; HMTc has not identified, and does not cite, any California provision applying Title 22 section 64431 maximum contaminant levels to bottled water sold in the state, so this cell must not be read as an assertion that California enforces 10 µg/L against a packaged product. Second, SOVEREIGNTY: California is a sub-national government. The only alternative anywhere in the register is the NHMRC Australian Drinking Water Guidelines statement that hexavalent chromium should not exceed 50 µg/L (nhmrc2025_crvi_drinking_water_50), which is five times looser and carries the same drinking-water scope hop; it is named here and not selected because the method takes the strictest applicable value. The value is unchanged from the earlier compilation at 10 µg/L; only the provenance tag is corrected, from regulatory-alignment to read-across. HMTc publishes Cr-VI as its own cell in addition to total chromium: a hexavalent result never satisfies the total-chromium cell and a total-chromium result never satisfies this one, and the total-chromium cell on this row is a direct sovereign maximum for the product form that bounds this species from above. Neither named instrument carves natural mineral water out of its own scope, but neither reaches packaged water of any kind, which is why this cell is a read-across on this row for the same reason it is one on the other three.
